whyThisMatters: Real incidents rarely look like a test. They arrive with a plausible reason, a deadline and a real business cost for saying no. The goal here is to practise a response that is safe and still keeps work moving.
rememberThis: STOP, VERIFY, REPORT. Pause before acting, confirm through a channel you already trust (never the one the request arrived on), and tell the right team. A good answer protects the company and keeps the business running.

discussionPrompts: For each case, ask the group to vote before revealing the answer. Notice how often two options split the room.
Ask: what did the best answer cost in time? Compare that with what the fastest answer could have cost.
For the CEO and vendor cases, ask what a trusted verification channel looks like in your team. Is the number on file actually kept somewhere you can reach it quickly?
For the 2am MFA prompt, ask why 'deny and go back to sleep' feels complete, and what is missing from it.
Ask whether anyone would feel comfortable challenging a senior person or a real client for a quick check. What would make that easier?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is choosing a half-measure that feels responsible, such as replying to the same thread, asking a colleague who sees the same fake, or fixing it alone and telling no one. A second, independent channel and a report are what actually break an attack. People also overcorrect by refusing everything, which fails the business-continuity half of the answer.

cases.title: The 2am Approval Prompt
cases.scenario: At 2am your phone buzzes with a sign-in approval request for your work account. You had a late deployment last week and sometimes work odd hours, so it might be a delayed session. Ten minutes later it buzzes again. You did not start any sign-in. MFA fatigue means an attacker repeats prompts hoping you will approve one just to make it stop.

decisions.prompt: A second prompt has just arrived and you are half asleep. What do you do?

options.text: Approve it once so the prompts stop, since it is probably a delayed login from last week
options.feedback: If it is an attacker who already has your password, you have just let them in. A prompt you did not start is never a delayed login. Approving to stop the noise is exactly what the attack depends on.

options.text: Deny it and go back to sleep, and mention it to IT if it happens again
options.feedback: Denying is correct, but waiting is not. Repeated prompts mean someone already has your password. Until it is reset and checked, the attacker can keep trying or use the same password elsewhere.

options.text: Deny the prompt, do not approve anything, and report it to IT or security straight away so your password can be reset and your account checked
options.feedback: Right. Denying stops this attempt. Reporting now lets IT reset the credential and review sign-ins before the attacker moves to a different method. A short after-hours report costs far less than a compromised account.

cases.debrief: STOP: never approve a prompt you did not start, however tired you are. VERIFY: the prompts themselves prove someone has your password. REPORT: use the security or IT out-of-hours channel, since a password reset and sign-in review is the fix. Being embarrassed about waking someone is the attacker's best friend.

cases.title: The Supplier Changes Bank Details Mid-Thread
cases.scenario: You are paying a regular supplier's invoice due tomorrow. In the middle of an ongoing email thread you have used for months, their accounts contact writes: "Our bank has changed because of an audit. Please use the new account for this payment. The updated details are attached." The reply is in the same thread, from the same name, and the supplier is genuinely waiting on this payment. Business email compromise often hijacks a real thread or a lookalike address.

decisions.prompt: The payment is due tomorrow and the supplier is important. What is the best step?

options.text: Pay the new account, since it is the same thread and the contact is familiar
options.feedback: Being in an old thread proves nothing. Attackers who control a mailbox or a lookalike domain reply into real threads. Payment to a wrong account is hard to recover.

options.text: Reply in the thread asking them to confirm the new details are correct
options.feedback: You are asking the possible attacker to verify themselves. They will confirm. This looks careful but checks nothing.

options.text: Call the supplier on the number already in your vendor records, confirm the change with a known contact, follow your bank-detail change procedure, and report the email to IT. If it cannot be confirmed in time, pay the old account or agree a short delay
options.feedback: Right. A call to a number you already hold is an independent channel the attacker cannot control. Following the change procedure and keeping the old details avoids a missed payment while the check completes.

cases.debrief: Bank detail changes are a classic high-value fraud. STOP before changing any payee. VERIFY by phone on a number from your own records, not from the email, and use your formal change process. REPORT the message to IT so the thread and the supplier mailbox can be investigated. A short delay almost never harms a supplier; a lost payment does.

cases.title: A Colleague's Account Sends Odd Links
cases.scenario: A colleague you work with closely messages you on chat: "Hey, can you check this doc for me quickly? Need your sign-off before the client call." It contains a link you do not recognise, and the wording is a little unlike how they normally write. They are normally responsive and you really are expecting some sign-off today. A compromised account can be used to send believable messages from a trusted person.

options.text: Open the link in a private window so it cannot affect your normal session
options.feedback: A private window does not stop a fake sign-in page from taking your login, or a download from running. It only changes what your browser remembers.

options.text: Ask them in the same chat whether it is really them
options.feedback: If their account is compromised, the attacker is the one answering. You will get a convincing yes. The check has to go through a channel the attacker does not control.

options.text: Do not click. Contact the colleague by phone or in person to confirm, and report the message to IT or the security mailbox. If they did not send it, tell them their account may be compromised
options.feedback: Right. A call or face-to-face check uses a separate channel, and the report lets IT block the link and protect other recipients. You also help your colleague recover their account quickly, and the sign-off still happens once confirmed.

cases.debrief: A trusted sender is not proof when accounts are compromised. STOP before clicking. VERIFY by a different channel than the one the message came in on. REPORT it, because the same message has probably gone to others, and your colleague needs to know.

cases.title: The Urgent Wire Request From the CEO
cases.scenario: You receive a message that appears to be from the CEO: "I am in a confidential acquisition meeting and cannot take calls. I need a same-day wire to a new advisory firm to secure the deal. Details to follow, please do not discuss it with anyone." The reason is plausible, because the company really has been discussing acquisitions. The writing style and signature look right. Pretexting means building a believable story to justify an unusual request.

decisions.prompt: The CEO is unreachable by call and the deadline is today. What is the best response?

options.text: Prepare the payment but hold it for approval, asking the CEO by message to confirm they really want it
options.feedback: Messaging the same channel only reaches whoever is behind it. A prepared payment under secrecy pressure also invites a mistake later in the day.

options.text: Pay it. A genuine confidential deal justifies breaking normal process, and refusing could damage the acquisition
options.feedback: Secrecy plus urgency plus a new payee is the standard shape of CEO fraud. Real deals still use the normal payment controls, and an authentic executive will back you for following them.

options.text: Pause, verify through a different route such as the CEO's executive assistant or a number on file, and follow the normal dual-approval process. Report the request to IT or security
options.feedback: Right. The EA or a known number is an independent route. Dual approval protects both you and the company, and if the request is real it will survive a ten-minute check. If not, you have stopped the loss.

cases.debrief: Authority, urgency and secrecy together are the strongest manipulation pattern. STOP regardless of seniority. VERIFY on a channel you choose, such as the assistant, a switchboard number or a face-to-face check, and use normal approvals. REPORT the attempt so finance and IT can watch for follow-ups.

cases.title: A Contractor Needs an Account Today
cases.scenario: A contractor starts today and the project lead emails you: "Please set up an admin account for Jordan right now. He is on a tight deadline and the client demo is this afternoon. I will sort out the paperwork later." The project lead is real and the demo is on the calendar. Least privilege means giving people only the access they need, for only as long as they need it.

decisions.prompt: The demo is hours away. What do you do?

options.text: Create the admin account now and chase the paperwork later, to avoid blocking the project
options.feedback: Unapproved, over-powerful access is how a small mistake becomes a big breach. 'Paperwork later' often means never, and nobody has confirmed the request or the person.

options.text: Refuse until the full onboarding process completes, however long it takes
options.feedback: The instinct to protect access is right, but a flat refusal ignores the business need. People then share logins or find workarounds, which is worse.

options.text: Confirm the request with the project lead by phone or ticket, give a standard least-privilege account with an end date for the specific systems needed, and complete the formal approval in parallel
options.feedback: Right. A quick independent confirmation, a time-limited account with only the needed rights, and approval done alongside keeps the demo on track and limits the damage if anything is wrong.

cases.debrief: Speed and security are not opposites if access is scoped. STOP before granting broad rights on an email alone. VERIFY with the requester through a trusted channel and the approver on record. REPORT the exception through your normal ticketing so it is visible and expires.

cases.title: Pasting Customer Data Into an AI Tool
cases.scenario: Your manager wants a quick analysis of 200 customer complaints before a meeting in an hour. The company's approved AI tool is slow and limited. A free public chatbot would do it in seconds if you paste the whole spreadsheet, which has names, emails and account numbers. Data entered into some public tools can be stored and reviewed, or used to train models.

decisions.prompt: You have an hour. What is the best approach?

options.text: Paste it all into the public tool. It is faster, and the customers will never know
options.feedback: You lose control of personal data the moment it is pasted. It may breach customer commitments and data-protection rules, regardless of whether anyone finds out.

options.text: Strip out names and emails and paste the rest into the public tool
options.feedback: Account numbers, dates and free-text complaints can still identify people. Partial redaction feels safe but is not a guarantee, and it is not policy-approved.

options.text: Use the approved tool even though it is slower, share only the columns you need, and if time is short ask IT or your manager about a faster approved route or a smaller sample
options.feedback: Right. Approved tools have contractual data protections. Minimising the data and asking for a faster route keeps the work moving without exposing customers.

cases.debrief: Treat public AI tools as outside the company. STOP before pasting anything non-public. VERIFY the tool is approved and the data is allowed to go there. REPORT to IT promptly if you have already pasted something, so the exposure can be assessed and not guessed.

cases.title: You Entered Your Password, Then Doubted It
cases.scenario: Ten minutes ago you signed in to a document-sharing page from an email. It looked like the usual one. Now, while preparing for a client presentation at 3pm, you notice the web address was slightly different and you are not sure it was genuine. Reporting means telling IT you may have made a mistake, and a password reset could lock you out just before the meeting.

decisions.prompt: The presentation is in two hours. What do you do?

options.text: Keep going and only mention it after the presentation, so it does not disrupt you
options.feedback: Attackers use stolen credentials within minutes. Two hours of delay is a long head start, and the presentation files may be the target.

options.text: Change your password yourself and say nothing, to avoid a fuss
options.feedback: Changing the password helps, but without a report IT cannot check for mail rules, active sessions or forwarded data. The attacker may already have a session that a password change does not end.

options.text: Report it to IT now, say exactly what you entered and when, and ask them to reset your credentials and review sign-ins. Tell them about the 3pm meeting so they can prioritise getting you access back
options.feedback: Right. A fast, honest report lets IT end sessions and reset access quickly, and your deadline helps them prioritise. Being open early nearly always costs less than a late discovery.

cases.debrief: Doubt after the fact is a signal, not an embarrassment. STOP using the account for sensitive work. VERIFY nothing yourself by hunting for evidence. REPORT immediately with specifics, because IT can fix most of this fast. Blame is rare; delay is what causes the damage.

cases.title: The Engineer With an Appointment
cases.scenario: You badge in at a secure door during the morning rush. A friendly person in a polo shirt carrying a toolbag says: "I'm from the air conditioning contractor, we have a booking for the server room corridor. Can you let me through? I'm already late." They know the floor and mention the facilities manager's first name. A queue is building behind them. Tailgating means following an authorised person through a secure door.

decisions.prompt: People are waiting and the visitor seems genuine. What do you do?

options.text: Let them through, since they know the facilities manager's name and the booking sounds real
options.feedback: A name and a toolbag are easy to acquire. Plausible detail is how pretexting works, and a stranger in a server corridor is a serious exposure.

options.text: Politely escort them to reception, where the booking can be checked with facilities, and let your colleagues go in. Report the attempt if the booking does not exist
options.feedback: Right. Reception can confirm the appointment against the visitor log and issue a badge and an escort. A genuine contractor loses a few minutes, and a fake one is stopped and reported.

options.text: Let them through but ask them to wait at the end of the corridor until you phone facilities
options.feedback: They are already inside, unescorted and unchecked. Verification must happen before access, not after it.

cases.debrief: Physical access is real access. STOP at the door, however busy. VERIFY the visit through reception or facilities using the booking system, not the visitor's own story. REPORT any unrecognised person who cannot be verified. A polite process is easy for genuine visitors to accept.

cases.title: IT Support Calls About Your Ticket
cases.scenario: Yesterday you raised a ticket because your laptop was slow. Today a caller says: "Hi, this is the IT service desk, I'm following up on your ticket about the slow laptop. To fix it I need you to approve the sign-in request I'm sending and install a quick remote-support tool." The caller knows your ticket subject, which is the thing that makes it convincing. Vishing is voice phishing carried out by phone.

decisions.prompt: The call matches something you really did. What do you do?

options.text: Approve the prompt and install the tool, since they clearly know about your ticket
options.feedback: Knowing the ticket subject only shows they have seen ticket data or guessed a common problem. Approving the prompt and installing remote software gives them full control of your laptop.

options.text: Politely end the call, then contact the service desk through the official portal or the number published internally and ask whether they called. Report the call
options.feedback: Right. You choose the channel, so the caller cannot control it. The real service desk can see their own ticket history and will happily confirm. Reporting helps IT block the number and warn others.

options.text: Ask the caller to prove who they are by reading you your ticket number, then proceed if it matches
options.feedback: Anything the caller reads out is something they could have obtained. Asking them to prove themselves keeps you on their channel instead of moving to yours.

cases.debrief: A caller who knows something true is not necessarily genuine. STOP before approving prompts or installing software for anyone who called you. VERIFY by calling back on a number you find yourself. REPORT it. Real IT will not mind a call-back.

cases.title: Files Are Suddenly Locked
cases.scenario: You are finishing an end-of-month report when files on your laptop and the shared drive start showing odd extensions and will not open. A message appears demanding payment to restore them and gives a short countdown. A team deadline is due in two hours and the report is nearly finished. Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment to unlock them, and it can spread across a network.

decisions.prompt: What is the best immediate action?

options.text: Switch the laptop off immediately and wait quietly to see whether it goes away
options.feedback: Powering off may destroy evidence that helps IT, and doing nothing leaves the shared drive exposed. The key problem is the network connection and the lack of a report.

options.text: Disconnect from Wi-Fi and the network cable so it cannot spread, leave the machine on, do not touch the ransom message, and call IT or security right away
options.feedback: Right. Disconnecting contains the spread while leaving the machine on keeps useful evidence in memory. A fast call lets IT isolate the shared drive and restore from backups. Do not pay or contact the attacker.

options.text: Try to save what you can onto a USB drive so you meet the deadline, then call IT
options.feedback: Copying files to a USB drive can carry the infection to other machines and it delays reporting. The deadline is important, but IT can usually restore files from backup.

cases.debrief: Containment comes before recovery. STOP working on the affected machine. VERIFY nothing by experimenting. Disconnect it from the network and keep it on. REPORT immediately, and never pay or negotiate on your own. IT will handle restoring files from backups, which protects the deadline better than improvising.
